rationale: A wins because its best angles are cleanly separated and fact-checked before a reporter does it for you. "Why local-currency reimbursement is the hard part of going global, not the card itself" finds the actual plumbing story without pretending Brex has market-share data; B's "Brex spends big on global infrastructure without saying if it's profitable" is a sharper thought, but "spends big" is an assumed cost story wearing a headline. B is useful, but A gives a founder safer, more pitchable routes with proof gates that would survive the first callback.
gaps_in_A: "category-creation" overstates what this is. A 50-country launch can support a category or consolidation story, but it is not category creation unless Brex can prove a new market is forming.
"the category is consolidating from per-region tools into a single global stack" is plausible, but not in the update. It needs outside market evidence before it becomes more than a tidy thesis.
A parks the money question in "Profitability is undisclosed..." but never develops the sober financial-scrutiny angle from the supplied $12.3B valuation fact.
gaps_in_B: "Brex spends big on global infrastructure" invents spend magnitude. The update gives scope, valuation, and undisclosed profitability, not buildout cost or burn.
"whoever proves global capability first" sneaks in a first-mover race the facts do not establish. That line will collapse the second Ramp says it already has coverage somewhere.

"cards and local-currency reimbursement live in 50 countries at once, not a phased pilot" assumes simultaneous full availability. The update says launching in 50 countries; it does not prove every market is equally live.

"The corporate-card feature CFOs of global startups actually asked for" over-narrows the protagonist. The fact says enterprise customers asked; it does not say CFOs, startups, or globally distributed teams were the source of the request.
